name: Digital Services Act
evidence_rating: thin: no promised indicators; enforcement record and descriptive transparency studies only; no causal evidence on economic or safety outcomes
summary: The DSA set no monitoring indicators, and its forecast 1-1.8% boost to cross-border digital trade has not been evaluated. Enforcement has begun - X was fined EUR 120m in December 2025 - and the new transparency database has made moderation more visible, but audits of hundreds of millions of records show platforms report inconsistently. No study yet measures the DSA's effect on illegal content, users' safety or the platform economy.

indicators.objective: The DSA proposal's financial statement contains no indicators section; monitoring was left to the Commission's evaluation under Article 91

indicators.indicator: Better protection of users and fundamental rights online; effective supervision
indicators.evidence: Enforcement under way: first non-compliance decision fined X EUR 120m (5 Dec 2025) for misleading verification, deficient ad repository and blocking researcher data access; other investigations ongoing. Transparency database operational but platform self-reports inconsistent.
indicators.sources: Commission decision Dec 2025; Kaushal et al.; Trujillo et al.

literature.citation: European Commission (2020), Impact Assessment accompanying the DSA proposal (executive summary SWD(2020) 349), SWD(2020) 348
literature.title: Impact Assessment accompanying the DSA proposal (executive summary SWD(2020) 349)
literature.headline: Cross-border digital trade expected to rise 1-1.8%; direct costs proportionate to size and reach; less legal fragmentation
literature.summary_plain: The Commission expected the DSA to raise cross-border digital trade by 1-1.8% by replacing diverging national rules.

literature.citation: European Commission (2025), First DSA non-compliance decision: X fined EUR 120 million, Decision of 5 December 2025 (as reported by eucrim)
literature.title: First DSA non-compliance decision: X fined EUR 120 million
literature.venue: Decision of 5 December 2025 (as reported by eucrim)
literature.headline: EUR 120m for deceptive 'blue checkmark' verification, inadequate advertising repository and refusing researchers access to public data
literature.summary_plain: The first DSA fine: EUR 120 million against X for misleading verification badges, an incomplete ad library and blocking researchers.

literature.citation: Kaushal, van de Kerkhof, Goanta, Spanakis & Iamnitchi (2024), Automated Transparency: A Legal and Empirical Analysis of the Digital Services Act Transparency Database, ACM FAccT 2024 (arXiv 2404.02894)
literature.authors: Kaushal, van de Kerkhof, Goanta, Spanakis & Iamnitchi
literature.title: Automated Transparency: A Legal and Empirical Analysis of the Digital Services Act Transparency Database
literature.method: descriptive (sample of 131m statements of reasons, Nov 2023)
literature.headline: Some transparency gains, but compliance problematic because the database lets platforms exercise wide discretion; terms-of-service grounds dominate over illegal content
literature.summary_plain: The DSA's public database of moderation decisions adds some transparency, but platforms report so inconsistently that it is hard to rely on.

literature.citation: Trujillo, Fagni & Cresci (2023), The DSA Transparency Database: Auditing Self-reported Moderation Actions by Social Media, arXiv 2312.10269
literature.title: The DSA Transparency Database: Auditing Self-reported Moderation Actions by Social Media
literature.method: descriptive (all 353m records from 8 largest platforms, first 100 days)
literature.headline: Platforms adhered only in part to the database's structure; structure partly inadequate; large cross-platform differences; database contents inconsistent with platforms' own transparency reports
literature.summary_plain: An audit of 353 million moderation records found the big platforms only partly comply with the DSA database and that their submissions contradict their own reports.

literature.title: Content Moderation on Social Media in the EU: Insights From the DSA Transparency Database
literature.method: descriptive analysis of 156 million Statements of Reasons in the DSA Transparency Database over two months
literature.outcomes: frequency, grounds, automation and type of moderation decisions by platform
literature.headline: TikTok made more than 350 times more moderation decisions per user than X/Twitter; most decisions were automated, while X reported relying solely on manual methods.
literature.summary_plain: Using the EU's new database of platform moderation decisions, the authors found platforms report in very different ways, which suggests the DSA is being applied unevenly.
literature.period_geography: Sept-Nov 2023; EU, eight very large social media platforms
literature.quality: Large-scale measurement of self-reported data; early window; no causal design.
literature.citation: Chiara Drolsbach, Nicolas Pröllochs (2023), Content Moderation on Social Media in the EU: Insights From the DSA Transparency Database, arXiv:2312.04431 (cs.SI)

literature.authors: Daria Dergacheva, Vasilisa Kuznetsova, Rebecca Scharlach, Christian Katzenbach
literature.title: One Day in Content Moderation: Analyzing 24 h of Social Media Platforms' Content Decisions through the DSA Transparency Database
literature.venue: Lab Platform Governance, Media and Technology (ZeMKI), University of Bremen, technical report
literature.method: descriptive analysis of one day of Statements of Reasons from eight VLOP social media platforms in the DSA Transparency Database
literature.outcomes: volume, automation and categories of moderation decisions
literature.headline: The eight platforms reported over 2 million moderation decisions in one day, about 68% automated, while X declared no automated decisions at all.
literature.summary_plain: A snapshot of one day of data that big platforms must send to the EU shows millions of moderation decisions, mostly automated, and big inconsistencies between how platforms describe them.
literature.period_geography: One day in autumn 2023 (with checks on 4 and 10 Oct); EU
literature.quality: One-day snapshot, descriptive; useful early compliance evidence only.
literature.citation: Daria Dergacheva, Vasilisa Kuznetsova, Rebecca Scharlach, Christian Katzenbach (2023), One Day in Content Moderation: Analyzing 24 h of Social Media Platforms' Content Decisions through the DSA Transparency Database, Lab Platform Governance, Media and Technology (ZeMKI), University of Bremen, technical report

literature.authors: Benedetta Tessa, Gautam Kishore Shahi, Amaury Trujillo, Stefano Cresci
literature.title: When Transparency Falls Short: Auditing Platform Moderation During a High-Stakes Election
literature.venue: EPJ Data Science (2026), doi:10.1140/epjds/s13688-026-00704-8; arXiv:2604.19285 (earlier version arXiv:2504.06976)
literature.method: time-series analysis of 1.58 billion self-reported moderation actions in the DSA Transparency Database by eight largest platforms over eight months around the 2024 European Parliament elections
literature.outcomes: changes in moderation volume and strategy around elections; data quality
literature.headline: Across 1.58 billion moderation actions, platforms' self-reported enforcement patterns did not change significantly around the 2024 European Parliament elections, and transparency gaps persisted a year after the database launched.
literature.summary_plain: Platforms did not visibly change how they moderated content around the 2024 EU elections, according to the data they must report under the DSA, and that data still has big gaps.
literature.quality: Large-scale interrupted-time-series style measurement; relies on self-reported data whose structure may hide changes.
literature.citation: Benedetta Tessa, Gautam Kishore Shahi, Amaury Trujillo, Stefano Cresci (2026), When Transparency Falls Short: Auditing Platform Moderation During a High-Stakes Election, EPJ Data Science (2026), doi:10.1140/epjds/s13688-026-00704-8; arXiv:2604.19285 (earlier version arXiv:2504.06976)

literature.authors: Amaury Trujillo, Benedetta Tessa, Stefano Cresci
literature.title: Disarranged Harmonization of Transparency Reporting by Social Media Platforms Under the Digital Services Act
literature.method: large-scale quantitative data-quality analysis of transparency reports and database submissions of the eight largest platforms after the Commission's harmonised reporting templates, plus structured comparison
literature.outcomes: compliance and data quality of DSA transparency reporting (formatting, timeliness, consistency, completeness)
literature.headline: After the Commission's harmonisation rules, all eight platforms still showed problems in data formatting, timeliness, consistency and completeness, and some submitted contradictory information across reporting channels.
literature.summary_plain: Even after the EU standardised how platforms must report their moderation, the reports remain messy, late or inconsistent, making them hard to check.
literature.period_geography: 2025-2026; EU, eight largest social media platforms
literature.quality: Systematic measurement of compliance; no causal design; preprint.
literature.citation: Amaury Trujillo, Benedetta Tessa, Stefano Cresci (2026), Disarranged Harmonization of Transparency Reporting by Social Media Platforms Under the Digital Services Act, arXiv:2605.17655

literature.authors: Marie-Therese Sekwenz, Ben Wagner, Hans De Bruijn
literature.title: From Reports to Reality: Testing Consistency in Instagram's Digital Services Act Compliance Data
literature.venue: ACM Journal on Responsible Computing (doi:10.1145/3821526); arXiv:2507.01787
literature.method: multi-level consistency analysis of Instagram's DSA compliance data (transparency reports, database, other disclosures); case study
literature.headline: A multi-level consistency framework applied to Instagram's DSA reporting can detect potential compliance failures across interconnected reporting channels (abstract gives no headline numbers).
literature.summary_plain: By cross-checking the different reports Instagram must publish under the DSA, the authors show inconsistencies that can flag possible compliance failures.
literature.quality: Single-platform case study; method-focused; abstract lacks quantitative results.
literature.citation: Marie-Therese Sekwenz, Ben Wagner, Hans De Bruijn (2025), From Reports to Reality: Testing Consistency in Instagram's Digital Services Act Compliance Data, ACM Journal on Responsible Computing (doi:10.1145/3821526); arXiv:2507.01787

literature.title: TikTok, child safety, and the Digital Services Act: An empirical analysis of online harm mitigation
literature.method: descriptive and cross-tabulation analysis of 11.6 million TikTok Statements of Reasons from the DSA Transparency Database at four time points in 2024-2025
literature.outcomes: TikTok moderation actions for protection of minors
literature.headline: Across 11.6 million TikTok moderation records, content flagged under 'Protection of Minors' is a significant share of moderation activity.
literature.summary_plain: TikTok's own DSA reports show that a large part of what it removes or restricts is flagged as harmful to children.
literature.quality: Descriptive, single platform, self-reported data; abstract seen via Semantic Scholar metadata.
literature.citation: Adriana Mutu, L. Pătraș (2026), TikTok, child safety, and the Digital Services Act: An empirical analysis of online harm mitigation, Communications (De Gruyter), 2026, doi:10.1515/commun-2025-0120

literature.authors: Manuel Tonneau, Diyi Liu, Ryan McGrady, Kevin Zheng, Ralph Schroeder, Ethan Zuckerman, Scott A. Hale
literature.title: Language Disparities in Moderation Workforce Allocation by Social Media Platforms
literature.venue: ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability and Transparency (FAccT 2026), doi:10.1145/3805689.3806484
literature.method: cross-platform audit of human moderator staffing by language using DSA-mandated transparency report disclosures, six platforms, relative to content volume
literature.outcomes: moderator coverage and workload by EU language
literature.headline: DSA disclosures reveal large cross-language disparities: millions of EU users on smaller platforms such as X post in languages with no dedicated human moderators, and per-moderator daily decision volumes differ by more than an order of magnitude across languages.
literature.summary_plain: Using staffing data platforms must publish under the DSA, the study finds content in some languages gets far less human moderation than English, leaving some users less protected.
literature.period_geography: 2023-2025 DSA transparency reports; EU, six major platforms
literature.quality: Novel use of DSA transparency data; descriptive; depends on accuracy of self-reported staffing numbers.
literature.citation: Manuel Tonneau, Diyi Liu, Ryan McGrady, Kevin Zheng, Ralph Schroeder, Ethan Zuckerman, Scott A. Hale (2026), Language Disparities in Moderation Workforce Allocation by Social Media Platforms, ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability and Transparency (FAccT 2026), doi:10.1145/3805689.3806484
